title: Nine Days of the Year
one_line_summary: A shrine sweeper who has rung the four o'clock bell since she was nine is thrown out of the sanctum for touching it on a paying day — and then learns that nine days of the year were her grandmother's, were sold for eleven hundred rupees, and that in law a turn of worship cannot be sold.
engine: The god must be worshipped every day forever, and every single day of the circuit belongs to one named human who officiates and keeps everything given that day — so the calendar itself is heritable property, the family multiplies faster than the calendar does, and there is no year in which someone's turn is not being taken from them.
why_this_works: It sells the underestimated one. The mechanism is a real legal object that most listeners have never had named for them: a hereditary turn of worship — pala in Bengal, osra in Rajasthan — which the Supreme Court has held is immovable property, and which the Supreme Court has separately held cannot be transferred by sale for money. Put those two holdings side by side and the entire show falls out of them: the paper that dispossessed kesar's family is the same paper that proves it never happened, and jorawar's power rests on a stack of documents that are strong socially and worthless legally. The listener understands the trap by episode four. kesar does not understand it until episode eight. That gap is the show. After that the question stops being 'was she cheated' and becomes 'how many of the other five houses were cheated the same way, and what happens to a village where every day of the year is suddenly in dispute.' The climb is audible because the shrine is audible: episode 1 she is dragged off the bell rope in front of the fair; episode 9 she rings it and nobody moves; episode 14 the same crowd hears her name read first on the board. And every reversal is public by construction, because a turn of worship is a thing you exercise in front of a courtyard full of people or you do not hold it at all.

protagonist.who: Twenty-four. Sweeps the shrine of Baba Ghanteshwar at Barkheri, lights its ninety-one lamps, rings the four o'clock bell. Has done it unpaid since she was nine because her mother did it before her. Listed on the seva board as sevika, which is not a share of anything.
protagonist.wants: To be paid once. Then, after episode six, to hold a day — one day of the five hundred and forty — in her own name where it can be read out.
protagonist.ashamed_of: That her mother begs. That she has taken food from the shrine kitchen for fifteen years and has never once been asked to sit down to eat it.
protagonist.does_not_know_at_start: That her grandmother mohari held nine days of the Barkheri circuit; that in 1968 those nine days were passed to jorawar's father by a deed that says the word 'sold' and names eleven hundred rupees; and that a turn of worship cannot be sold for money and cannot pass unregistered — so the nine days never left her family, and every rupee taken on those nine days for fifty-seven years was taken from her.

antagonist.who: Sixty-two. Holds two hundred and fourteen of the five hundred and forty days. Chairs the shrine committee. Addressed as manager sahib by men older than him. Has never raised his voice in the courtyard and has never had to.
antagonist.wants_incompatibly: The circuit re-cut and sealed at the next full moon with the whole calendar consolidated in one hand — his — before anyone thinks to ask which of his fifty-one transfers were ever registered.

timeline.what_happened: The shebaiti right of a family shrine passed by written transfer between unrelated men twice in sixty years — from the founder's line to Srimanta Pandit in 1820, and to Shashi Bhusan Banerjee in 1880 — establishing that the office was being treated in practice as transferable property.
A widow, Pramila Debi, sold a half-share of the temple property and the shebaiti right to Upendra Nath Ganguli for Rs 1,200, pleading legal necessity arising from litigation expenses.

At the temple of Kalyanji Maharaj, Diggi, district Tonk, the hereditary office was held in rotating turns — called osra in Rajasthan, pala in West Bengal — of ten days each within an eighteen-month circuit; during her turn the holder officiated as pujari and received all offerings made at the temple. In that year Mst. Acharaj executed an unregistered deed purporting to pass her osra to another.

The Supreme Court held that neither the temple nor the deities nor the shebaiti right can be transferred by sale for pecuniary consideration; the doctrine of legal necessity reaches the temporality only, never the office.

The Supreme Court held that a hereditary office of shebait enjoyed by turn is immovable property; the 1961 deed, being unregistered, was inadmissible in evidence and the claim founded on it was dismissed.

The Supreme Court held that a shebait is duty bound to protect the property of the temple and cannot usurp it for his own gain; a shebait family occupying temple land was found to be unauthorised occupants rather than tenants, and the revenue entry was ordered to remain in the temple's name.

Contests over who may officiate at a temple, and therefore over who receives what is given there, continue to be fought as hereditary-right litigation; a man who trained eighteen months as an archaka was arrested in September 2015 for demanding appointment, the certification being stayed by court.

_timeline_note: Seven entries because the record supports seven. The mechanism is sourced; Barkheri, the shrine of Baba Ghanteshwar, the five hundred and forty day circuit, the nine days, the 1968 deed and every person in the season are invented. Nothing in `season` is restated here.

_people_note: Short, and it should be. The record for this mechanism is judgment text: it names litigants and nobody else. There is no reported modern Barkheri and no living private individual behind kesar, jorawar, mohari or the 1968 deed. Filling this list further would have meant inventing people into the clearance section, which is the one place invention is not allowed.

season.turn: On the fair morning kesar rings the four o'clock bell as she has for fifteen years, and jorawar has her pulled off the rope in front of the fair crowd for touching it on a paying day.
season.ends_on: Her name is scraped off the seva board with the knife they use for coconuts, while the fair queue watches.

season.turn: bhanwari goes to jorawar's gate to beg, and what she begs for is not her daughter's place.
season.ends_on: bhanwari does not ask him to put kesar back on the board. She asks him not to open the 1968 page.

season.turn: sitara arrives from Jhilan to buy days ahead of the re-cut and hires kesar for forty rupees a day to walk her round the shrine and read the roll aloud.
season.ends_on: sitara's list has nine days on it with no holder's name written against them.

season.turn: girdhari, who has been feeding kesar answers, carries her questions to jorawar to keep his post as ledger-keeper.
season.ends_on: jorawar says the number nine to kesar before kesar has said it to him.

season.turn: jorawar comes to bhanwari's door with a courtesy: the seva roll can be rewritten tonight if bhanwari signs a paper stating her mother-in-law never held a turn.
season.ends_on: The paper already carries bhanwari's thumbprint at the bottom, from something she signed nineteen years ago.

season.turn: kesar makes girdhari read the 1968 page aloud in the shrine office in front of tejmal, rukmani and the committee, and he cannot get through it without saying the word and the figure.
season.ends_on: girdhari says the name mohari out loud, then says to tejmal: nine days, and they were hers.
season.pays_off: Who struck her name off the board and why. The 1968 page is read out, the word 'sold' and the figure eleven hundred rupees are said in public, and kesar's grandmother is named for the first time in nineteen years.

season.turn: jorawar announces the circuit will be re-cut and sealed at the next full moon and that any claim must arrive registered, in writing, before then.
season.ends_on: Twenty-two days. And the deed kesar needs was drawn by the same pleader who drew every deed jorawar holds.

season.turn: kesar reaches phoolchand's almirah in Jhilan and gets the 1968 deed in her hands.
season.ends_on: The deed says sold, for eleven hundred rupees, and it carries no registration stamp of any kind.

season.turn: kesar takes the bell rope at four in the morning on one of the nine days and rings it, and tejmal stands beside her and does not stop her, because his own scattered sixty-one days rest on the same rule.
season.ends_on: tejmal calls it kesar's ninth in front of the committee, and rukmani writes it into the day-book that way.

season.turn: bhanwari tells kesar what she put her thumb to nineteen years ago.
season.ends_on: The paper bhanwari signed was not about the nine days. It was kesar's birth entry, and the father's column on it carries tejmal's name.
season.pays_off: Why bhanwari begged instead of fought, and what she has been protecting for nineteen years. The thumbprint from episode five is explained, out loud, by the woman who made it.

season.turn: sitara, who has already paid for days that cannot lawfully be sold, turns on kesar and gives her six days to make the rule stick in the register or be named as the forger of the ledger entry.
season.ends_on: sitara has paid jorawar four lakh sixty thousand rupees in cash for eleven days, and holds no receipt for any of it.

season.turn: at the sub-registrar's office hukum refuses to accept jorawar's re-cut papers, because a turn of worship is immovable property and not one of jorawar's fifty-one transfers was ever registered.
season.ends_on: hukum reads the entry aloud — nine days, Barkheri circuit, in the name of kesar, granddaughter of mohari — and jorawar has to sign the register as witness to it.

season.turn: tejmal takes jorawar's offer — sixty-one continuous days across the fair — and swears an affidavit that mohari surrendered the nine days verbally before 1968.
season.ends_on: tejmal's affidavit puts him in mohari's room in April 1968, and the deed in kesar's hand is dated the January before it.

season.turn: On the fair morning, one year to the day from episode one, in the same courtyard and in front of the same crowd, the circuit is re-cut on the evidence: tejmal's affidavit collapses on its own date, sitara produces what she paid, hukum's register stands, and jorawar's two hundred and fourteen days are reduced to the eleven he can prove.
season.ends_on: The board is rewritten in front of the fair. The first line reads: kesar, nine days, by right of mohari.
season.pays_off: Everything. The nine days return and are registered. jorawar says kesar's name and her turn out loud in front of the crowd that watched her dragged off the rope. bhanwari's thumbprint is cancelled in open committee and tejmal acknowledges the birth entry where the courtyard can hear it. sitara's four lakh sixty thousand is ordered returned out of jorawar's fair collections. girdhari reads the new roll. narmada gets her apology in the courtyard she asked for. chhotu is given the second bell day with his name against it. phoolchand's 1968 deed is produced, read and impounded.

reasons: The mechanism is drawn from reported judgments. The individuals named in those judgments are litigants from 1907 to 1978 and are dead; they appear in `people` for clearance only and none of them is a character.

Barkheri, Jhilan, the shrine of Baba Ghanteshwar, the five hundred and forty day circuit, the nine days, the 1968 deed and every person in `cast` are invented. No real shrine, village, family or turn-holder is depicted.

The living-person exposure in this material sits in ongoing hereditary-priesthood litigation, which is also where the communal and caste-political charge sits. The season is deliberately kept inside one family's calendar arithmetic: no community is set against another, no caste claim is adjudicated, and the antagonist and protagonist are of the same house.
Only the seven `timeline` entries come from the record. Everything tagged `reported` is rendered as something a character asserts, never as narration.

_novelty_note: Searched for film, serial and web-series adaptations of turn-of-worship / pala / osra / shebaiti disputes and found none. The adapted neighbours in this space are hereditary-priesthood caste dramas and temple-treasure stories, neither of which uses the calendar-as-property mechanism.

fictionalization_map.osra / pala — hereditary turn of worship: kept, as 'the turn' and 'the circuit'; the mechanism is the one thing not renamed
fictionalization_map.ten-day turn in an eighteen-month circui: five hundred and forty days, cut into turns of unequal length
fictionalization_map.Pramila Debi, widow who sold a half-shar: mohari (composite); the sale figure becomes eleven hundred rupees in 1968
fictionalization_map.Ram Rattan, claimant under the transferr: jorawar's father, offscreen; jorawar inherits the claim

never_narrate_as_fact: That mohari ever agreed to give up the nine days — tejmal asserts it in episode 13; the narrator never states it.
That the 1968 money was actually paid to mohari rather than to someone else in the house — jorawar asserts it; girdhari doubts it.
That bhanwari knew what she was putting her thumb to in the birth entry — bhanwari says one thing about it in episode 10 and jorawar says another in episode 5.
That any of jorawar's other fifty-one transfers were fraudulent as opposed to merely unregistered — sitara asserts it, hukum only ever says 'not registered'.
_sources_note: Every URL above was opened during this hunt. Four returned readable content and carry the timeline entries. livelaw was paywalled, latestlaws returned only the citation header, the spotlaw PDF returned binary, and the Rayagada report belongs to a rejected candidate — none of those four is cited for any fact.

also_considered.title: The nephew who buried his uncle on paper
also_considered.one_line: An old man walks into the tehsil office to pay his land tax and is told he cannot, because he died last year and his nephew inherited.
also_considered.why_rejected: Engine 6. The mechanism is a single forged mutation entry; once the entry is corrected the story is over, and the best-known version of it has already been filmed.

also_considered.title: The offering box nobody may open
also_considered.one_line: Priest and committee each put a lock on the temple door and the god goes unfed for eleven days.
also_considered.why_rejected: Good sound, no ladder. One standoff, no climb, and no protagonist with anywhere to climb from.

also_considered.title: Eighteen months in a coma
also_considered.one_line: A family tells the neighbours he is only sleeping, and every morning the wife pours river water on him.
also_considered.why_rejected: Blocked on register, not on engine. It requires depicting a mentally unwell woman and a real named dead man, and the strongest version of it makes an audience of her illness.
